description: Rhineland county (c. 963–1443) whose dynasty produced four Holy Roman Emperors, Henry VII, Charles IV, Wenceslas, Sigismund, making it one of the most politically influential houses of the late medieval Empire despite its modest territorial base in the Ardennes.

lifecycle_phases.description: Sigefroid builds the castle on the Alzette; Luxembourg identity coalesces.
County grows through Rhineland marriages and inheritance.
Henry VII becomes emperor; Luxembourg dynasty at the height of its European influence.
Line weakens; county sold to Burgundy 1443.

rise_factors.description: The Luxembourg dynasty produced four Holy Roman Emperors, giving the county exceptional imperial prestige and resources.
Tight integration with imperial politics gave Luxembourg leverage in Rhineland and Bohemian affairs.
Consistent dynastic transmission through the 12th–13th centuries built a stable institutional base.

The Luxembourg family produced four Holy Roman Emperors (Henry VII, Charles IV, Wenceslaus IV, Sigismund). This imperial connection gave a small Moselle county extraordinary political reach, including the acquisition of Bohemia (1310) which became the dynasty's primary resource base.

Luxembourg's position at the Ardennes fortifications, the "Gibraltar of the North", made it strategically critical for controlling movement between France, Germany, and the Low Countries. This military geography gave the county leverage beyond its agricultural resources.

The Luxembourg dynasty produced four Holy Roman Emperors (Henry VII, Charles IV, Wenceslaus, Sigismund) between 1308 and 1437, making the county the dynastic anchor of imperial power and its count consistently among the most influential princes in Europe.

decline_factors.description: Philip of Saint-Pol sold Luxembourg to Burgundy 1443 to pay dynastic debts, ending independence.
Post-1346 line required repeated female succession and dynastic transfer.
Luxembourg resources spread across Bohemia, Hungary, and the Empire rather than consolidated at home.

Luxembourg was sold to Philip the Good of Burgundy (1443) when the Luxembourg dynasty's main branch died out. Subsequent Habsburg inheritance meant Luxembourg became a strategic frontier province rather than an independent polity.
